new.definition: Bananas cooked in a pan of butter, brown sugar and cinnamon with banana liqueur, then flamed with rum and spooned warm over vanilla ice cream. It was created in 1951 at Owen Brennan’s Vieux Carré restaurant on Bourbon Street in New Orleans and named for a friend of his, the chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission. At Brennan’s it is made and flamed at the table, for two or more.
new.guest: Bananas Foster was created by Brennan’s in 1951. We cook the bananas in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon with a little banana liqueur, flame them with rum right here at your table, and spoon them warm over cold vanilla ice cream. It is made in one pan, for two or more of you.
new.kitchen: The cart goes out set with the pan, the burner, the butter, sugar, cinnamon, liqueur, rum and bananas, the rum measured into a small vessel before it comes near a flame. Who flames it, and the house procedure, are set by the manager at lineup; on Thanksgiving Day the sheet listed the tableside flambé as an addition to the three course menu.
new.compare: Its nearest neighbor is crêpes Suzette, the other classic dessert flamed at the table: there thin crêpes are warmed in a sauce of caramelized sugar, butter, orange juice and zest and flamed with an orange liqueur. Bananas and rum over ice cream, against crêpes and orange liqueur, are the tell.

new.background: Bananas Foster was created in 1951 at the Vieux Carré, the restaurant Owen Brennan (1910 to 1955) ran on Bourbon Street before the family business moved. He asked for a new dessert made with bananas and named it for his friend, the chairman of the New Orleans Crime Commission. Bananas were close at hand: the house’s own history tells of a surplus at the family’s produce business, and New Orleans was then a major port of entry for bananas from Central America. Accounts differ on whose hands made it. The house credits its chef of the day, and the family’s telling credits Ella Brennan (1925 to 2018), Owen’s sister, with him, drawing on a banana dish their mother made at home. After Owen’s death the restaurant moved in 1956 to 417 Royal Street, and the dessert went with it.

new.definition: To flame a dish: a spirit such as rum, brandy or cognac is added to the warm pan and lit, and it burns briefly over the food. What burns is the alcohol vapor above the pan, and the flame goes out by itself once the vapor is spent. Much of the alcohol stays behind: in the USDA’s retention figures a flamed dish kept about 75 percent of its alcohol. The word is French, the past participle of flamber, to flame or singe.
new.guest: Flambé means flamed: the rum goes into the warm pan and we light it, and it burns for a moment over the bananas while the caramel deepens. It is a show, and it is flavor too. The flame does not burn off all the alcohol, so if you are avoiding alcohol, please tell me.
new.kitchen: The spirit is measured into a small vessel first, never poured from the bottle near a flame, and added with the pan pulled off the heat; the far edge of the pan is then tilted to the flame to light it, away from the server and the guests, and the flame burns out before the plate is made. No alcohol ever goes into a pan that is already alight.
new.compare: Its nearest neighbor is brûlée, as in crème brûlée: both are named for fire, but a brûlée crust is sugar scorched until it browns, with no spirit at all, while a flambé is a spirit set alight in the pan. Alcohol and a live flame are the tell.

new.background: Flambé is French for flamed, the past participle of flamber, to flame or singe, and Merriam-Webster dates the word in English to 1914 as an adjective and to about 1946 as a verb. The usual story of the flamed dessert, that crêpes Suzette caught fire by accident in the 1890s at the Café de Paris in Monte Carlo, comes from the memoir of the waiter who claimed it, and it is disputed: Larousse Gastronomique contradicts it, and other accounts credit other Paris restaurants. New Orleans kept flamed classics of its own. Café brûlot, coffee with brandy, spices and citrus peel set alight at the table, is credited to Antoine’s in the late nineteenth century, and Bananas Foster, flamed with rum at the table, joined it at Brennan’s in 1951.

new.definition: A small movable side table or cart drawn up beside the guest’s table, on which a server carves, dresses, finishes or flames a dish in the guest’s view. Guéridon service is the name for this way of serving: the dish is made or finished at the table rather than plated in the kitchen, and the cart often carries a small burner. In furniture the word is older: a guéridon is a small round pedestal table, first made in France in the seventeenth century.
new.guest: The cart we bring beside your table is called a guéridon, a French word for a small side table. Everything for your Bananas Foster is on it, the pan, the burner, the butter and sugar, the bananas and the rum, so you can watch your dessert made and flamed right beside you.
new.kitchen: The cart is set from the kitchen before it goes out, with the burner, the pan, the measured spirit and every ingredient, so the server never leaves the table in the middle of the dish. It is placed where nothing hangs overhead and away from drapes and paper, with a lid within reach to smother a flame.
new.compare: Its nearest neighbor is the dessert trolley, which wheels finished desserts to the table to be chosen: a guéridon is a working station on which the dish is cooked, carved or flamed. Whether the food is made on it, not merely carried, is the tell.

new.background: The guéridon began as furniture. It appeared in France as a small pedestal table in the seventeenth century, and its early supports were often carved as standing figures: a print in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, from a seventeenth century book of guéridon designs, shows one as a pedestal in the form of a Moor. The name is usually traced to Guéridon, a stock character of seventeenth century French farces and popular songs, though the origin is not settled. In restaurants the word passed to the side table or cart on which a waiter carves, dresses and flames dishes beside the guest. The practice grew out of service à la russe, the course by course service that reached Paris early in the nineteenth century, in which dishes were carved on a side table and handed round by the waiters, course by course.

new.definition: A frozen dessert of cream, milk and sugar, churned as it freezes so that air is whipped in and the ice crystals stay small. In the United States the FDA’s standard of identity requires ice cream to carry at least 10 percent milkfat, and a version richer in egg yolk may be labeled frozen custard or French ice cream. The air whipped in is called overrun: premium ice creams carry little of it and eat dense, while light, fluffy ones carry more. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it was the vanilla bean ice cream under the Bananas Foster.
new.guest: Under the Bananas Foster is vanilla ice cream, cold and creamy, and the warm bananas and rum caramel are spooned straight over it. That meeting of hot and cold, as the ice cream just begins to melt into the sauce, is the heart of the dish.
new.kitchen: The ice cream is scooped just before the bananas and sauce go over it, so it softens under the warm sauce at the table and not before. Which ice cream goes under the Foster, the housemade vanilla the regular menu prints or the New Orleans Ice Cream Co. vanilla bean the Thanksgiving sheet printed, is the chef’s to confirm at lineup.
new.compare: Its nearest neighbor is gelato, which usually carries less butterfat than ice cream’s legal floor of 10 percent, has less air whipped in because it is churned more slowly, and is served warmer, so it eats denser and softer. More cream and more air are the tell of ice cream.

new.background: The earliest known ice cream recipe recorded by an American is in the hand of Thomas Jefferson (1743 to 1826): a vanilla ice cream, undated but most likely written down during his years in France in the 1780s, now held by the Library of Congress. Monticello’s own historians note that the popular claim that he introduced ice cream to the country is false; he is credited only with that first recorded recipe. In 1843 a patent was granted for an artificial freezer, cranked by hand, that made it far easier to churn at home. In 1851 a Baltimore milk dealer began making it wholesale, the start of the American ice cream industry. The United States later set a legal standard of identity for it, with its floor of 10 percent milkfat.

new.definition: The pairing of chocolate with orange, carried as zest, candied peel, juice or an orange liqueur. The bright, slightly bitter orange lifts the weight of cocoa, and the pairing is an old one: seventeenth century chocolate drinks were already scented with orange flower water. Its classic confection is the orangette, a strip of candied orange peel dipped in dark chocolate. On the Thanksgiving Day menu it was the Chocolate and Orange Tart, with candied hazelnuts.
new.guest: Chocolate and orange is an old partnership: the bright, slightly bitter orange keeps rich chocolate from feeling heavy. Our Chocolate and Orange Tart sets the two together in a tart, with candied hazelnuts for crunch, a holiday chocolate dessert for the end of a big meal.
new.kitchen: Orange can go into a chocolate dessert as zest steeped in the cream, as candied peel, as juice or as an orange liqueur. How the tart carried its orange, and how dark its chocolate was, was the pastry kitchen’s to say at lineup.
new.compare: Its nearest neighbor is the orangette, the same pairing as a confection: candied peel coated in chocolate, eaten by hand. In a tart the chocolate is the body and the orange the accent; in an orangette the orange peel is the body and the chocolate its coat. Which one is the body is the tell.

new.background: Chocolate met orange soon after it reached Europe. In 1652 a London translation of a Spanish treatise, printed as Chocolate: or, An Indian Drinke, gave a recipe for the drink that listed orange flower water among its flavorings, beside sugar, long red pepper, cloves, aniseed and almonds. Confectioners later made the pairing solid in the orangette, a strip of candied orange peel dipped in dark chocolate, a classic of French chocolate making. In England, Terry’s of York launched its Chocolate Orange in 1932, a ball of orange flavored chocolate shaped like the fruit, after a Chocolate Apple it had made from 1926. On the Thanksgiving Day menu at Brennan’s the pairing came as a tart, finished with candied hazelnuts.

deepen.background: Caramel came into English in the early eighteenth century from French, which took it from Spanish caramelo, and dictionaries trace it back through Portuguese to a Late Latin word for a small reed, calamellus; a medieval Latin name for sugarcane, cannamella, is thought to have shaped it along the way. The chemistry came later. Table sugar, sucrose, begins to caramelize at about 160 to 170 C (320 to 338 F), while fructose, a sugar of fruit and honey, browns at about 105 to 110 C (221 to 230 F). Time matters as well as heat: held long enough, sugar can caramelize below its melting point. In a Bananas Foster the butter and brown sugar melt into a pan caramel before the bananas go in.
deepen.metAt: Brennan's Thanksgiving Day 2026: the pan caramel of World Famous Bananas Foster, the candied hazelnuts of the Chocolate and Orange Tart and the candied pecans of the Sweet Potato Agnolotti
deepen.guest: Caramelized means the sugar has been cooked until it browns, turning plain sweetness into something toasty, nutty and a little bitter. In the Bananas Foster the butter and brown sugar cook into a caramel right in the pan at your table, and the candied nuts on our desserts wear a thin caramel coat.
